Their evidence wasn't capable of proving genocide. And the third year they come back to you again and you still say, Well, you never know, give it a try, and they're rejected, just as the Prosecution's evidence was rejected in the Krajisnik case in 2006. Then some international body comes along and says that people with your sons and daughter's grades aren't qualified for Harvard, just like the International Court of Justice said that what happened in the municipalities doesn't qualify for genocide. And then your son or daughter comes back to you after all of that and says, Am I capable of getting into Harvard, and I think at that point, much as you would love your child, it would be reasonable and maybe even prudent to say, No, you're not capable of getting into Harvard. And that's what the Trial Chamber did here. They told the Prosecution in 2012 after all of these decisions, after these events had been scrutinised so many times: Your evidence is not capable of proving genocide. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Robinson, you are finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Well, since we are ahead of time, I think we will now turn to the Prosecution for a reply. Or, actually, yes, I mean we could use the next 20 minutes and we will have a break. No use now to have a break now. So why don't you start and then we will have a break at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was going to suggest a break, Mr. President, in part because my LiveNote wasn't working, so I couldn't revert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was going to suggest a break in part because the normal transcript availability wasn't technically available here, so I couldn't scroll back to arguments that were being made. I think it would be -- from our point of view it would be more efficient if we could break now and then resume following consultation. Obviously I'm not rejecting what the Court wishes to do, but I think that would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: All right, but could I ask you just to stay in your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. We will now adjourn for 20 minutes, which means we will reconvene at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Before we go to the Prosecution, Judge Robinson, I believe that you had a point still to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a clarification. Mr. Robinson, in your submissions you made reference to the well-known appellate rule that the Appeals Chamber pays deference to the findings of the Trial Chamber, but that of course relates to findings of fact. What is being said here is that the Trial Chamber made an error of law in its application, in its interpretation and application of Rule 98 bis, but of course the deferential principle has no application in relation to errors of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would respectfully submit that what has been raised as questions of law don't go to the issue of whether they apply 98 bis correctly, but they go to other issues such as the serious bodily harm for actus reus which is not dispositive of this appeal but the issue that's actually in contention whether there was evidence capable of supporting a conviction, that's the -- that's the question that the Prosecution is disputing. They say they have evidence capable of supporting a conviction. We say they didn't. That to me is a question of fact and a question of evaluation of evidence. That in all of your decisions, whenever you evaluate evidence from a final judgement, you apply the deferential standard to. So I don't see how you could distinguish this situation from an appellant, an accused, who was convicted after a trial and says that they applied the standard of beyond a reasonable doubt incorrectly, because, in fact, the evidence showed that there was reasonable doubt. The Prosecution is saying the same thing here, that the evidence showed that there was evidence capable of sustaining a conviction for genocide, and I think that you have to apply the same deferential standard that you do in the situation of appeal from a final judgement of conviction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... the situation, but if we find that they have misunderstood the meaning of 98 bis then that really, to my mind, is a question of law, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if you -- yes, if you find that they applied the wrong 98 bis standard and -- as in Jelisic you could reverse on that basis as a question of law, but I question how you could read the Trial Chamber's decision and all of the approach that it took and find any error in its methodology for 98 bis. Maybe you disagree with their conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, there's no error in the articulation. The articulation is a hundred per cent correct. It's where I have difficulties is in the application of those principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Robinson. Before giving the floor to the Prosecution, I have a question to ask of Mr. Tieger, if I may. I believe that earlier today and on page 30 and 31 of your brief you identified a statement by Mr. Karadzic in Exhibit D92 where you claim he said that, and I quote, "This conflict was aroused in order to eliminate the Muslims." I have looked at this exhibit, and my understanding is that Mr. Karadzic was stating that there was truth in the statement that Europe had aroused the conflict in order to eliminate "the Muslims." If I am correct about this context, would you still claim that the full statement of Mr. Karadzic taken at its highest is evidence that Mr. Karadzic possessed genocidal intent? And I'm not speaking of other statements. I'm speaking of this one specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't dispute the context, either the factual context of the discussion in the Assembly or the general backdrop that you have identified, although I don't have the statement in front of me at this moment. What I would emphasise, however, is that in attributing responsibility for the initiation or outbreak of the conflict to the Europeans or to the European Community, that does not in any way gainsay the nature of the destructive acts that were unfolding thereafter. In other words, it is not a matter of suggesting that somehow it is the Europeans whose forces are engaged in the process of eliminating Muslims, but instead it is that a further iteration of claims seen in other context by Dr. Karadzic, that we have been forced by circumstances to do what we are doing; in this case to eliminate the Muslims who are vanishing. And they're vanishing as the context of this Assembly session makes clear in just the manner I described in my submissions earlier. They're vanishing by virtue of their placement in detention facilities with horrific conditions. They're vanishing as a result of attacks on their communities resulting in massive killings, and they are vanishing as a result of the various acts that have been described before. So sorry to be a bit long-winded, but what I mean is the -- again focusing on the Europeans' alleged responsibility does not undercut the intent related to the acts being perpetrated by Mr. Karadzic's forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Still I think we would all agree that it would have been preferable to cite exactly what Mr. Karadzic said and not have an approximation. I understand your explanation. Yes, Judge Liu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, I think I'm not very much assisted by Mr. Robinson's answer to my question, so I would like you to articulate your response on your understanding of the review of the procedure in the 98 bis. Is it the reasonableness or beyond a reasonable doubt? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Liu. Let me do two things quickly. Let me foreshadow that this was a matter I believe Ms. Jarvis intended to respond to in greater detail, but I certainly would respond immediately to your inquiry by saying that I think you've identified precisely the distinction that exists. This is that the difference is between -- the difference between 98 bis and the determination at the conclusion of trial embraces the difference that Judge Robinson referred to repeatedly during his colloquy with Mr. Robinson, and that is the difference between assessing all the evidence at the conclusion of the trial to determine whether or not it rises to the level of proving the allegations beyond a reasonable doubt and the dramatically different standard that exists at the 98 bis stage for very good reasons when the matter proceeds by way of brief oral argument without the full explication of written briefs and without a full assessment of the totality of the evidence, and the standard there is whether or not there is any evidence capable of supporting conviction. As I say, Ms. Jarvis may address that in greater detail, but I think you have identified an important distinction that the Defence submissions tried to blur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I have one more question to you, Mr. Robinson. I am looking at Prosecution Exhibit 3405, paragraph 95, and I will read it to you: Witness statement said that he met with Sveto Veselinovic, a municipal leader, who told the witness that he had meetings with Karadzic where: "It had been decided that one-third of Muslims would be killed, one-third would be converted to the Orthodox religion, and one-third will leave on their own, and thus the Muslims would disappear from the territory." A statement like that, doesn't it provide direct evidence of genocidal intent?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Now the question is whether it was ever acted upon or whether the genocide ever actually took place. So that is evidence which taken at its highest could be considered evidence of genocidal intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Okay. Now we are at reply by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. We can be very brief in reply. We just have a few points we wanted to highlight arising out of the respondent's submissions today and picking up on some of the questions that Your Honours have also asked in the course of the hearing. And the first thing I wanted to address is the standard of review issue for a Rule 98 bis appeal. Mr. Robinson in his submissions suggested that we hadn't addressed it in our submissions today, but we've certainly addressed this issue at length in our appeal briefs and in particular our reply brief at paragraph 20, and the reason why we don't emphasise it in the hearing today is that we, at the position we take, is that the law is very much settled on this. There really is no discussion to be had. The Jelisic Appeals Chamber, that the Chamber first seized of a Rule 98 bis appeal, set the matter out very clearly and we've described the relevant holding from the Jelisic Appeals Chamber at the end of paragraph 20 of our reply brief. So we say the Appeals Chamber, Your Honours, may reverse the Chamber's decision if it determines that there was evidence which could have provided a basis for any reasonable Trial Chamber to find the accused guilty of the offence charged. And of course in applying that legal proposition, we also take into account the prohibitions on weighing evidence and picking and choosing amongst the evidence. So we say that's clear. We see no basis for limiting the Jelisic holding in any way. There's nothing in that finding that suggests it would not equally be applicable to the Rule 98 bis appeal in this case here today. Of course the respondent's submissions in relation to the Rule 98 bis standard are also very much bound up in the notion that there were no legal errors made by the Trial Chamber in the course of assessing count 1. For us it is important to bear in mind that not only were there Rule 98 bis application errors as clearly evidenced by their language, the language of taken in light of and notwithstanding, but there were also legal errors in its approach to the elements of genocide. And it is the confluence of those two things that have led us to such a problematic place in the outcome in relation to count 1. Your Honours, the second point I want to mention, and in some respects I hesitate to mention it, but it is the ICJ decision, and I won't spend long on it. We of course would fully endorse the comments that Your Honour Judge Robinson has already made about why this case is not helpful to us in this particular circumstance. First of all, it's not a criminal proceeding. It wasn't dealing with the individual criminal responsibility of a single accused person, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, which is what this Tribunal is dealing with here. The ICJ didn't have the same evidence of the direct statements that Dr. Karadzic made that we have evidence in our case, so even on the basis of the evidence considered it's not comparable. In terms of the standard as Your Honour Judge Robinson has very eloquently described, it was a different standard being applied by the ICJ, and it is a higher standard than the one that is applicable at the Rule 98 bis stage. They were looking to see whether they were fully convinced of the position being put forward by the applicant. It necessarily involves weighing the evidence, the type of assessment that will have to be made at the end of this case but not at the Rule 98 bis stage. And of course as Mr. Robinson has acknowledged, the ICJ decision was very heavily bound up in what this Tribunal had said on the final question of genocide, not at the 98 bis stage, but at the end of -- at the end of the proceedings in other cases. Well, Your Honour, that begs the question of what this Tribunal is going to do in this case in relation to the genocide charge for Radovan Karadzic. So for all of those reasons our strong position is that the ICJ genocide case is of little assistance, particularly at the 98 bis stage. The third point I want to mention is the argument made by the respondents that we don't have -- we might have independently the actus reus, we might have independently the mens rea, but we don't have the confluence of those two things. Your Honours, we submit precisely the opposite. We say here what you need is the confluence of the actus reus and the mens rea in relation to the accused person in question, and that is exactly what the evidence on record supports. The only way you reach the conclusion that Mr. Robinson proposed is if you fall into the objective genocide trap. If you separate out the question of what was Dr. Karadzic's intent and you look for evidence of an objective genocide on the ground. So, Your Honours, there really is no basis for saying that we don't have the necessary confluence of actus reus and mens rea required for criminal responsibility in this case. My fourth point is that of course, again and as within the brief, the respondent is making much of the fact that so far the Prosecution at this Tribunal has not succeeded in proving genocide in the municipalities to the standard applicable at the end of the case. Obviously that is the situation, but it's not correct to say that the Prosecution hasn't come quite close, and I would point you to the Stakic appeal decision where the Appeals Chamber accepted, in fact, that in relation to Prijedor municipality, the Trial Chamber's factual findings could be enough to sustain a conviction for genocide but it wasn't prepared to say under the standard of deference that the Trial Chamber was wrong to reach another conclusion. So let's not be too hasty in thinking that the Prosecution's genocide charge for 1992 has been very easily and lightly dismissed. It hasn't. But of course what is much more important is what has happened at the 98 bis stage, applying the 98 bis standard. And there, Your Honours, the Prosecution has succeeded every time. And if you follow that same pattern, if you apply the standard correctly there is no basis for reaching a different conclusion in this case. Indeed as Mr. Tieger said how would we explain to the victims that other accused like Slobodan Milosevic could be held at the 98 bis stage to answer for a charge of genocide based on Dr. Karadzic's statements, at least in part, and yet we don't ask Dr. Karadzic himself to answer to those same charges. And then finally, Your Honour, obviously everything the respondent has suggested in terms of the 98 bis standard and the final conclusion reached in this case depends upon a weighing of the evidence. In answer to Your Honour Judge Meron's question just now about whether the particular statements of Dr. Karadzic that you mentioned taking at its highest would be sufficient, he said yes. That is an extraordinary concession, Your Honour, in the context of the Rule 98 bis standard. It is only by misapplying the standard that we reach the conclusion that the Trial Chamber reached. I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Robinson added something to the yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Robinson again, what he added, shows that what he is relying on is a weighing of the evidence. What he is suggesting is that you simply have to look and see whether weighing all of the competing factors it's enough to sustain a genocide charge. And we say that's the fundamental problem, that's the question for the end of the case, as Your Honour Judge Robinson has pointed out numerous times. It would, Your Honours, just to conclude, be unbelievably problematic for this Tribunal to prematurely terminate count 1 at this stage of the proceedings. It really is one of the fundamental questions arising out of the criminal campaign in Bosnia in 1992, and that's a question that deserves the fullest most careful consideration by this Tribunal based on the full evidentiary record and full argument by the parties. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and I would like to express my appreciation to the parties for the brevity and focus of their arguments today which makes the very difficult task of the Appeals Chamber a bit easier. Now, the question is whether Mr. Karadzic would like to make a personal statement. Up to ten minutes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellencies. Good day, and I highly appreciate this opportunity to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Just a second. We must switch to translation. Try now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellencies. I would like to express my gratitude for this opportunity to address you. However, with your leave, I believe that my advisor, Mr. Robinson, did leave some of his time to me, so I hope you will allow me to speak for more than ten minutes altogether in view of the time that was left over by Mr. Robinson. I do understand that today at this session it is not probative value that is being discussed. I'm not a lawyer, and from that point of view I fully rely on my exceptional advisor Mr. Robinson and his associates. Also on the fact that the Trial Chamber and this Chamber are not jury-based courts so therefore I don't have to engage in a performance that would -- being that I was trying to persuade someone of something. That's why I'm going to address you the way an honourable man addresses honourable people. Although I'm not a lawyer, better than anyone else in the world I know the factual state of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I know also what my responsibility was. It's not only that I know what I did. I also know what I thought, what I wanted, what I was saddened by, what I worked for - I and my associates - and I had insight into their thoughts and actions, too, and intentions. I am not going to speak now about my not being guilty of genocide as mentioned in count 1. I'm trying to say that no one was responsible for genocide because genocide did not happen. There could not have been a war crime without war, and the Trial Chamber has an abundance of evidence showing that the Serb side led by yours truly -- and I personally made every effort to prevent a war. Once the war happened, it broke out where the other side wanted it to break out. In most municipalities where war happened, that war broke out for six weeks after the war broke out in Sarajevo; that is to say for four or six weeks they managed to preserve the peace in those areas that were Serb controlled. In most municipalities there was no war. There were no crimes. Entire settlements, purely Muslim from the beginning until the end of the war remained as they were, and they do remain to this day. Even in those municipalities where there were conflicts and where there were crimes, as is the case in a civil war, there were purely Muslim or purely Croat villages that were not put in harm's way at all. So it was not religious affiliation or ethnic affiliation that led to crime and problems. Where there was fighting there were crimes, and we will agree that the Serb side did not have any interest in having armed conflicts happen within its territory. That would have been insane, and after all, that would not involve criminal liability because the feeble-minded cannot be held accountable. There are villages deep in Serb territory that remained intact. Different allegations and constructions of the Prosecution to the effect that we were against the Muslims do not hold water. With the Muslim leaders of a European orientation, we had agreements and we made every effort to have peace. We gave up on all our plans in the interest of preserving Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole within Yugoslavia and our life together with Muslims, and in such a state there would have been as many Muslims as there were Serbs almost. While I was in politics, and I'm a physician and a writer, not a politician, I gave hundreds of interviews, hundreds of statements. I issued hundreds of documents, orders, decisions, but the Prosecution cannot find a single consistent paragraph that would give even a bit of context that would identify genocidal intent on my part or any kind of intent. His Excellency Judge Meron noted very well what was missing in that citation. It was my speech made on the 15th of October, 1991, at the joint Assembly that was cited. It is an eminently antiwar speech. I'm not trying to persuade the Muslims to go to war. I'm trying to dissuade them. Even what was shown here was antiwar. I am dissuading all three ethnic communities. I'm telling them not to go to war, and I'm offering concessions in order to preserve the peace and in order to avert the danger of war. The highest representatives of the international community, like the late Cyrus Vance -- the Prosecution has the document of the 8th of March, 1992, that states that Karadzic is prepared to do his best to avert war at all costs. However, what was not played for your Excellencies from this speech of the 15th of October, 1991, is D1270, pages 122 to 124 in Serbian and in English pages 116 to 118, and this is what I say there: "I have to clarify a particular matter that stems from the interpretation of what we are saying at this rostrum. This actually pertains to the question of war and peace. I must repeat for the hundredth time that Serbs are not threatening with war," and so on and so forth. And then is says: "Serbs never attacked Muslims, nor will they ever attack Muslims, or is there any kind of feeling of that kind vis-a-vis the Muslims." Let me stop this citation now and let me say that the Serbs consider the Croats to be their main enemy, and they consider the Muslims to be Serbs of Muslim faith or at least we are of the same ethnic roots. And now I go on quoting: "The chaos that would be caused by irregular decisions of out-voting, the chaos that could happen, the chaos that no one would start but that has the logic of its own and we all spoke about that, it's not chaos that is in our hands. It is order that in our hands. This chaos could lead to a situation that would be ungovernable by anyone." And then on the next page, I say that: "... it be made public to the entire world tonight that Serbs, Croats, and Muslims do not wish to have war. So our message would be that there will be no war, and in that way we can guarantee there would be no chaos because order is in our hands and chaos is no longer in anyone's hands."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not have the text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber also had in mind my speech made in January 1992 where I accepted the proposals of the Muslim side to postpone the referendum and that we should go for referendum once regionalisation is over. The distinguished lady Prosecutor said today when she responded that you did not have all the statements at your disposal. However, what you did say does not confirm what they said. The Trial Chamber did have all of that when they made their decision. They had what you do not have, so those who made the decision had all of that. What the Prosecutor showed today does not confirm what they're trying to say. Also, brief statements were quoted, especially what his Excellency Meron noted. I am not pleased to see war. I am saddened by war. I am not pleased to see Muslims suffering and Muslim victims. I am saddened by it, and I am sad that their leadership is leading them along a path that leads to the suffering of us all, and them in particular. So as far as mens rea is concerned, and I have already adopted the term by now, in thousands of documents, my speeches, my interviews they could not find a single trace of any genocidal intent. In the documents that I issued during the war, 80 per cent, around 80 per cent of these documents are documents about restraint, about cessation of hostilities, about the passage of humanitarian aid, assistance to all three communities, especially civilians. There is no trace whatsoever of any genocidal intent. In the documents that the Assembly adopted that belong to the Assembly, to the legislation, there is not a single document, a single norm that would discriminate against Muslims and Croats. However, when we take all of that together, when we leave that aside, if you will, on the ground there was no genocide. Excellencies, no, there was no genocide, because the war was where the other side wanted it to happen, where fighting was caused. That's what the Trial Chamber had at their disposal. That's where chaos happened. The state was always against crimes. The Trial Chamber could see that when a perpetrator commits a crime he is already afraid of the first next level. For example, if it is a guard that commits a crime, he's afraid that the shift leader might see that, and so on and so forth. So this is far below me and far away from me. There were a lot of perpetrators of crimes. So it's between the perpetrators of crimes and myself. There are many, many instances and these perpetrators were afraid already of the first instance. They didn't want their supervisors to find out. And there is an abundance of such evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you would come to conclusion. I gave you some extra time already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I got carried away. I thought that I would be able to take up the time left over by Mr. Robinson. Mr. Robinson didn't mention that the Prosecution expert said what the percentage was among the Muslims that suffered or perished over the five years, but among the Serbs it was about 2.5 per cent, because the Serbs waged a war against the Croats and against the Muslim forces led by Mr. Adzic. Your Excellencies, there was no genocide. There were crimes, but the state was working to prevent them and punish them, and the Chamber will see that over time these efforts only increased and served as a confirmation proving what I say is correct and the Prosecution case is wrong. Thank you, Your Honours. I have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Let me again thank the parties for the work they have done on the case and the presentations they have done today. Let me thank my colleagues on the Bench, also thanks to the Registry and to the interpreters for their excellent assistance. The hearing is now concluded and the judgement of the Appeals Chamber will be delivered in due course, and we are adjourned.
